competition_series: FSAE-Australasia (FSAE-A) and Formula Student Germany (FSG); originally targeted FSG 2020 (cancelled due to COVID-19)
summary: Monash Motorsport began its driverless program in early 2018, prompted by FSG launching its first driverless competition class the prior year, and retrofitted autonomous systems onto their existing 2017 electric competition chassis to create M19-D - Australia's first student-built, fully autonomous race car, publicly unveiled in August 2019. Their planned competition debut at FSG 2020 was cancelled by COVID-19, delaying real competition validation by roughly three years. The team ran two vehicles (a driven car and a separate driverless car) until 2023, when they unified into a single dual-purpose car, M24, capable of both driven and autonomous racing. M24 demonstrated Australia's first competition-ready driverless AV demo at FSAE-A in December 2023, then took the program to Europe in 2024, finishing 7th of 30 Driverless entries at FSG (one of only 3 teams to complete all four Driverless dynamic events) and 6th in Hungary, with an overall FSG placing of 14th of 79 teams (494.52 points). A next vehicle, M25, is planned to return to Europe in 2026.
dv_program_start: Early 2018 (per team's own account: the driverless project began after FSG ran its first driverless competition class in 2017, prompting Monash Motorsport to add a third car project)

first_dv_competition: Formula Student Germany 2020 was the original target (vehicle was declared 'competition-ready'), but FSG 2020 was cancelled on 22 March 2020 due to COVID-19, so the team's first actual driverless competition start was FSAE-Australasia, December 2022 (per the team's own account of 'two successful Driverless demonstrations at Australasia' in 2022-2023), with the first fully competition-ready public AV Demonstration in December 2023.

ramp_phases: Concept and initial build on retrofit chassis (2018-2019, ~18 months to public demo)
Competition-ready but COVID-delayed (2020-2021, ~2 years lost to pandemic)
Dual-vehicle operation - separate driven and driverless cars (2018-2023, ~5 years)
what_slipped: The single largest slip was external and unavoidable: FSG 2020 (the team's target competition debut, for which the car was declared competition-ready) was cancelled due to COVID-19, pushing real competition validation back roughly 2-3 years to FSAE-Australasia Dec 2022/2023. Separately, running two entirely separate vehicles (one driven, one driverless) from 2018 to 2023 appears to have been a resourcing drag the team itself corrected by unifying into a single dual-purpose car (M24) in 2023 - implicitly acknowledging that maintaining parallel driven and driverless platforms was not sustainable long-term for a volunteer student team.
platform_prerequisites: Yes - M19-D was explicitly built by retrofitting a suite of autonomous systems onto the team's existing 2017 first-generation driven electric competition vehicle, rather than a purpose-built DV chassis. The EV base vehicle itself took roughly 1-2 years of prior development (program described as 'over three years in the making' by 2019, implying EV work started around 2016).
ebs_design: [uncertain] Search-aggregated sources describe 'pneumatic braking and safety systems' as part of the autonomous pipeline (alongside Jetson AGX Xavier compute, PSoC, RES, and a steering servo motor), suggesting a pneumatically-actuated EBS consistent with common FSAE-DV practice, but this was not confirmed via a primary document read directly and should be treated as moderate-to-low confidence pending the full VTE/design-report PDF.
steering_actuation: Steering actuator located at the steering rack: a rack-parallel ball screw driven by a brushless servo motor, coupled to the rack via a cross-bore and shoulder screw. The ball screw's low friction and lack of self-retention allows manual steering in manual (driven) mode; the assembly is removable via eight bolts plus the shoulder screw. Performance: full lock-to-lock steering in 0.4 seconds, providing 2000 N at the rack while stationary, matching a human driver's performance ~99% of the time versus historical Autocross telemetry. This satisfies the DT.2.2-style requirement for a decouplable actuator that permits both manual and autonomous steering.
brake_actuation: [uncertain] Distinct service-brake actuation for normal autonomous driving not separately confirmed from EBS braking in public sources; 'pneumatic braking and safety systems' referenced generally as part of the pipeline.
sensor_mounting_packaging: [uncertain] Not confirmed in detail; publicly described sensors (LiDAR, stereo/mono camera, IMU/GPS/magnetometer) are referenced generally without confirmed mounting locations from sources reviewed.
chassis_impact: M19-D chassis was a retrofit of the existing 2017 driven-EV monocoque. M24 (2023) represented a full redesign: a new carbon-fibre monocoque with distinctive aerodynamics purpose-built to support both driven and driverless operation in one chassis, plus widespread electrical changes for European regulatory compliance.
compute_platform: [uncertain, moderate confidence] Main autonomous-pipeline compute described (in aggregated secondary sources, not independently verified via a primary document) as an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier paired with a Programmable System-on-Chip (PSoC) for lower-level I/O/safety logic, alongside a RES (Remote Emergency System) module. This corresponds to the earlier M19-D/M22-era pipeline; the M24-era (2023-2024) compute platform was not separately confirmed.
sensor_suite: State sensors: IMU, GPS (~10cm accuracy), magnetometer. Observation sensors: LiDAR (Baraja Spectrum-Scan, adopted following an April-August 2021 evaluation/comparison against a previous LiDAR unit whose model was not identified in sources reviewed) and camera(s) (stereo camera pair in the M19-D era; by 2024 the team describes cone detection as 'LiDAR based... completely colour blind,' implying the M24-era perception pipeline may rely primarily on LiDAR geometry rather than camera color classification - a notable strategy difference from most peer teams). [uncertain] exact 2024-era camera/LiDAR model list.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: [uncertain] Referenced generally as 'a safety-critical monitoring system... continuously checking the car's heartbeats to ensure all systems and pressures were functioning as expected' (2024 Foxglove case study), but specific DS/remote-stop/EBS relay wiring per DT.4 not confirmed from primary sources.
remote_stop_system: A 'Remote Emergency System (RES)' is named as a core pipeline component in aggregated secondary-source descriptions of the M19-D/M22-era architecture; vendor/model not confirmed. [uncertain]
software_stack: ROS (version not confirmed as ROS1 or ROS2 - see ros_version field) running on Linux, structured into perception, localisation/mapping, motion planning, and control packages per the team's own design-report description of 'essential robotics problems including perception, localisation, mapping, motion planning and control.'
ros_version: [uncertain] Robot Operating System (ROS) confirmed as the software framework, but sources reviewed did not specify whether ROS1 or ROS2 (or which distro) was used in any given season.
perception_approach: M19-D/M22 era: YOLOv3 object detector with a PeleeNet backbone (chosen for inference speed) for cone detection from camera imagery, combined with LiDAR-based distance/geometry measurement and stereo-vision distance estimation. M24 era (2024): team describes their approach as 'LiDAR based cone detection, completely colour blind' per their own FSG team profile, suggesting a shift toward LiDAR-geometry-driven detection with reduced or no reliance on camera-based color classification of cone type by that point. [uncertain] exact detection range achieved.
slam_localization_approach: EKF-based SLAM: sensors can be individually enabled/disabled; cone detections from perception are treated as landmarks continuously added to the map relative to the vehicle's estimated pose; data association performed via Euclidean/Mahalanobis distance gating between detected and mapped landmarks; loop closure reconciles repeated observations of the same landmark to correct drift. [uncertain] which specific state variables (IMU-only vs. GPS-fused) were used in competition versus testing.
planning_approach: [uncertain] Not confirmed in detail from sources reviewed; the team's own design-report description references 'motion planning' as a core pipeline stage generating steering-angle and velocity requests from the SLAM-built map, implying a mapped-track path-generation approach, but the specific algorithm (Delaunay triangulation, midline, spline) was not identified.
control_approach: The Actuation subsystem converts high-level Motion Control requests into low-level steering, acceleration, and braking commands, and also facilitates safety systems; specific lateral/longitudinal control algorithm (pure pursuit, Stanley, MPC) not confirmed from sources reviewed. [uncertain]

data_logging: Foxglove WebSocket used for live multi-viewer telemetry during testing/competition (3D visualization of LiDAR point clouds, car position, planned path, and motion-control overlays, eliminating the need for engineers to huddle around one monitor); ROS bag files used for post-session recording and offline replay/analysis, adopted ahead of the 2024 European campaign.

critical_path_items: 1) The COVID-19 cancellation of FSG 2020 was the single largest schedule disruption, removing the team's planned first competition validation entirely and pushing real dynamic-event experience out roughly 2-3 years. 2) Consolidating from two separate vehicles (driven + driverless) to one unified car (M24, 2023) was clearly a resourcing/critical-path correction - maintaining two full vehicle programs in parallel for ~5 years (2018-2023) likely diluted engineering effort available for driverless-specific maturation. 3) Perception sensor maturity/choice - the team invested in evaluating and switching LiDAR technology (Baraja Spectrum-Scan, 2021) mid-program, and by 2024 had shifted to a LiDAR-centric, camera-color-independent detection strategy, indicating perception approach was iterated significantly rather than fixed early.

Competition-facing validation proceeds through standard FS scrutineering plus an 'Autonomous Vehicle Demonstration' dynamic event, which the team first completed successfully at FSAE-A in December 2023. The team's ability to complete all four Driverless dynamic events at FSG 2024 (one of only 3 of 30 teams to do so) is itself a strong positive reliability signal. [uncertain] whether any incidents occurred that were simply not publicly reported.
top_mistakes: [uncertain, inferred] No explicit team-authored 'mistakes' list was found. The clearest inferable mistake, based on the team's own subsequent correction, is running two fully separate vehicles (a driven car and a driverless car) in parallel from 2018 through 2023 rather than a unified platform - a structure the team itself abandoned in 2023 in favor of a single dual-purpose car (M24), implying the split-vehicle approach was judged inefficient with the benefit of hindsight. The multi-year gap between 'competition-ready' (2020) and actually completing a full Driverless dynamic-event slate (2024) also suggests the program underestimated how much additional validation work remained beyond initial competition-readiness claims, independent of the COVID disruption.

team_structure_dv: [uncertain, moderate confidence] Monash Motorsport overall spans roughly 100-130 student volunteers across all vehicle projects (aerodynamics, business, chassis/structures, dynamics, electrical, and autonomous systems). A current 'Autonomous Systems and Aerodynamics' team grouping lists 7 named members, though most listed roles (Head of Chassis, CTO-Mechanical, Head of Structures, Electrical Systems Manager) appear to be broader team leadership rather than DV-specific, with only one role explicitly titled 'Autonomous Software Engineer' - suggesting the true dedicated DV-software headcount is smaller than 7 and could not be precisely confirmed from public sources. Early in the program (2019), the driverless effort was one of three concurrent vehicle projects supported by roughly 130 total volunteers team-wide, with named leadership including a 'Driverless Chief Engineer' role.

recommended_sequence: Based on Monash's documented trajectory: 1) Retrofit driverless sensors and actuation onto an existing, already-sorted EV chassis rather than building new mechanical platforms simultaneously (as Monash did with M19-D on their 2017 EV base). 2) Get a public demonstration milestone early (Monash achieved a ~30 km/h open-day demo within ~18 months of program start) to build momentum and sponsor/institutional support even before competition entry. 3) Iterate perception sensor choice deliberately rather than locking in early - Monash re-evaluated and swapped LiDAR technology roughly 3 years into the program (2021) and again shifted detection strategy toward LiDAR-centric, camera-independent cone classification by 2024. 4) Unify vehicle architecture (driven + driverless in one car) as early as feasible rather than running two parallel vehicle programs - Monash's own 5-year detour running two separate cars (2018-2023) before consolidating into M24 is the clearest 'do this earlier' lesson from their history. 5) Build a repeatable, high-frequency on-track testing cadence (2-3x/week) with strong telemetry tooling (Foxglove + rosbag) ahead of any away competition, as this immediately preceded Monash's best-ever result (completing all 4 Driverless dynamic events at FSG 2024).
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Moderately applicable, with caveats: Monash's overall timeline (program start 2018 to first fully-completed Driverless dynamic-event slate in 2024, roughly 6 years) was heavily distorted by an external, non-repeatable event (COVID-19 cancelling their target debut competition), so raw duration numbers should not be copied directly. What IS directly transferable to a 24-month, ~9-person software-focused team with an existing EV: (a) retrofit onto the existing EV rather than building new mechanical structure, mirroring Monash's M19-D approach and QUT's QEV-3D approach; (b) prioritize a single unified vehicle architecture from day one rather than ever forking into separate driven/driverless cars, since Monash's own 5-year two-vehicle detour is presented here as their clearest structural inefficiency; (c) invest early in a strong telemetry/replay tooling stack (Foxglove-equivalent + bag logging) since Monash credits this workflow with contributing to their best-ever competition result; (d) consider a LiDAR-centric, less camera-color-dependent perception strategy as a valid alternative architecture worth evaluating, given Monash's apparent 2024-era shift in that direction, if the 9-person team is software-heavy and camera-pipeline maintenance (annotation, retraining, lighting robustness) is a bigger burden than LiDAR geometry classification.
